chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from the one who mentioned it, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:

When Allah intends goodness for a servant, He makes him ascetic in the world, gives him understanding in the Religion, and shows him its faults. And whoever is given these, has indeed been given the best of the world and the Hereafter.

And he said: 'No one seeks the truth by a door superior to asceticism in the world, and it is the opposite of what the enemies of the truth seek.' I said: 'May I be sacrificed for you, what is that [opposite]?' He said: 'Desire for it [the world].'
And he said: 'Is he not from the patient, generous ones? For indeed, it is only a few days. Indeed, it is prohibited for you to find the taste of faith until you are ascetic in the world.'

He said: 'And I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: When a believer isolates himself from the world, he soars and finds the sweetness of the love of Allah, and in the presence of the people of the world he is as if he has been mixed up, and indeed the people are mixed up by the sweetness of the love of Allah, so they do not occupy themselves with anything else.'
He said: 'And I heard him saying: Indeed, when the heart is cleansed, the earth becomes narrow for it until it soars.'

key_terms.الزُّهْدُ: Asceticism or detachment from the world
key_terms.تَخَلَّى مِنَ الدُّنْيَا: To isolate oneself from the world
key_terms.حَلَاوَةُ حُبِّ اللَّهِ: The sweetness of the love of Allah
key_terms.فَقَاهٌ: Deep understanding or jurisprudence in religion

ai.seo_question: What are the signs of Allah's goodness for a servant according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In Shia tradition, this hadith from al-Kafi frames zuhd not as mere renunciation but as a spiritual elevation where the heart becomes 'narrow' for the earth, allowing the believer to transcend material constraints. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) links this detachment directly to 'faqh fi al-din' (deep religious understanding), suggesting that intellectual and spiritual clarity are fruits of worldly disengagement. This concept of 'tasting' faith (dhawq) underscores the experiential nature of Shia gnosis, where love for God displaces attachment to creation.
